vignette: The air in Conference Center B still smells like ozone and spilled coffee to Eleanor, five years after the day the fire alarms never sound. She is seventy-two, consulting to architect a municipal fiber-optic backbone, her laptop open on a folding table when the doors burst open. She watches Marcus, a junior systems administrator she has mentored, drag a wounded colleague behind a vending machine. The thud of a body hits the carpet. The sharp, wet sound of breathing rises. She presses herself into a supply closet until the footsteps pass, her fingers leaving grease marks on the drywall she cannot move to wipe away. In the weeks that follow, Eleanor tells her husband she is fine over breakfast. She goes back to her office, reroutes emergency bandwidth, and files incident reports in clean, detached language. But her body keeps score. She stops sleeping through the night. When the furnace kicks on in their basement, her pulse spikes the same way it did in the closet. She begins auditing her home network at two in the morning, not because anything is down, but because watching the traffic graphs scroll feels like holding the world together by force of will. She avoids the downtown train line, then stops attending regional tech conferences altogether. “Too many uncontrolled variables,” she tells her project manager, then adds that she will shift to remote consultation. Now, Eleanor works from a sunlit corner of her library, three monitors reflecting the pale glow of firewall rules and packet captures. Her team relies on her ability to trace anomalies before they cascade, but her own systems no longer filter cleanly. A dropped call sends her to the door, peering through the blinds. A car backfires on the street below and her shoulders lock, her breath catching in that familiar, mechanical shallow rhythm. She traces the fiber connections behind her router with her fingertips, grounding herself in the predictable language of handshakes and acknowledgments. It helps. Not enough, but enough to keep the tremor out of her voice during client calls. Her marriage is steady, but the distance between them sometimes feels like a latency issue she cannot troubleshoot. Her husband leaves coffee on her desk, asks about her day, and waits while she reconstructs the morning in fragmented pieces. She finds herself apologizing for taking up space, for the sudden silences where her mind replays the weight of a backpack sliding across linoleum. She tells him she is grateful he is here, then immediately worries that her gratitude is performative, that she is forgetting what peace feels like without a checklist of contingencies. She no longer flinches at loud noises as violently, but the vigilance never fully dissolves. It settles into the quiet hours. She runs through evacuation protocols for coffee shops. She notices the structural weaknesses in older buildings—the single stairwell, the jammed emergency door. She has learned to name the panic when it rises: It’s a false positive. You are offline. You are safe. The words work, but they take time. She spends her days ensuring other networks never fail, while quietly rebuilding her own capacity to exist without bracing. When the screen finally goes dark at the end of the workday, she watches the reflection of her own face hover in the glass, breathing slowly, waiting for the signal that today has ended.
